strengths: UNOT offers a well-motivated combination of Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated training measures, and short Sinkhorn rollouts. Amortizing OT computation across datasets and resolutions without requiring converged training targets is a useful objective.

The reported computational gains are substantial on several benchmarks. Tables 1–2 show CIFAR reaching 1% transport-cost error in approximately 3 versus 80 iterations, with a 3.46-fold speedup. Cross-dataset pairs, resolution sweeps, and the variable-epsilon experiment provide additional evidence of transfer.

Proposition 5 provides a useful residual-to-potential error bound under positivity and centering assumptions. Predicting Sinkhorn initializations also permits subsequent iterative refinement when greater accuracy is required.

The paper supplies substantial background, architecture and training details, pseudocode, and a code-and-weights link. The barycenter and interpolation examples suggest applications beyond scalar cost prediction.
weaknesses: The advertised generator universality is not established for the implemented method. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and a Lipschitz constraint; Appendix C instead uses a 200-dimensional latent input for up to 8192 outputs and explicitly does not enforce that constraint. A manifold-hypothesis argument does not establish coverage of arbitrary discrete measures. Moreover, Corollary 4 is false as stated: G(z)=ReLU(z/2+1) satisfies the individual-layer assumptions, but G(G(z)) is always at least 1 and therefore cannot have positive density throughout the nonnegative domain. These are substantive limitations of a principal theoretical claim.

The OT formulations and learned variables need reconciliation. Equation (1) has the wrong sign for KL regularization, while Algorithm 1 reports only the linear transport cost under the same notation used for the regularized objective. More consequentially, the KL-based dual in Equation (3) requires scaling factors u=mu*exp(f/epsilon) and v=nu*exp(g/epsilon), whereas Proposition 1 omits the marginal factors. Consequently, the convergence result for those dual potentials does not directly apply to the learned epsilon*log(v) without an additional conversion. The KL sign is readily correctable, but the potential conventions affect the theoretical justification.

The geometry computations contain algorithmic issues beyond missing quantitative evaluation. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to a probability vector minus its gradient; this is not a simplex projection and does not preserve a nonuniform optimum even when its gradient is zero. For example, softmax([0.8,0.2]) is approximately [0.646,0.354]. Appendix A.4 also omits the derivative of the outer self-interaction term in the Sinkhorn divergence. Corrected algorithms, agreement with the implementation, and aggregate barycenter/geodesic errors are needed; a few visual examples and one GeONet trajectory do not establish the claimed geometric accuracy.

The comparisons do not adequately establish state-of-the-art initialization performance. The closest learned baseline, Amos et al. (2022), is excluded because of asserted distribution dependence, although a matched comparison at fixed resolution is feasible. Gaussian-initialization timings are also excluded, and speedups quoted from other papers cannot substitute for measurements under the same hardware and implementation. The observed gains over default Sinkhorn remain valuable, but are narrower evidence than the headline claim; UNOT is slower on MNIST.

The evaluation does not isolate the contributions of adversarial generation and the bootstrapping loss. Controlled comparisons against fixed synthetic generators and direct dual-objective training would clarify which components produce the gains, particularly given the 35-hour, 200-million-sample training investment. Proposition 5 bounds prediction error by a residual; it does not establish convergence of the detached adversarial optimization or guarantee that every residual reduction improves ground-truth error. These gaps, together with the correctness concerns above, make rejection more appropriate in the current version.
